question: In a black-box post-processing model where a learner may linearly combine group-transformed copies of any function, how many group-action queries are necessary to enforce exact symmetry versus a prescribed multiplicative reduction of the nonsymmetric L2 component?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines averaging complexity as support size of a universal, input-independent affine combination of group-action queries, and defines weak and strong approximate symmetry through contraction of squared L2 asymmetry.
key_findings.evidence: An averaging scheme is a real group signal whose weights sum to one; its size is the count of nonzero weights. Weak enforcement contracts asymmetry averaged over a uniform group element, while strong enforcement requires the left-hand inequality for every group element. Because the displayed quantities are squared L2 norms, the paper's epsilon corresponds to a norm tolerance of square-root epsilon.

key_findings.claim: Exact symmetry has averaging complexity |G| only after the faithful base class is enlarged through sufficiently high symmetric tensor degree; it is not a lower bound for every original function class.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 13 states AC_ex(gSym^⊗k(F)) = |G| for k at least K, with K bounded by min{|G|, sum over representation eigenvalues M_lambda minus 1}. For coordinate permutations acting on linear functions, degree d(d+1)/2 − 1 suffices. The paper itself gives constant functions as a class with exact complexity one.

key_findings.claim: For every finite-dimensional function class, approximate symmetry admits a universal random construction using O(log |G| / epsilon) action queries, with stated constants 8/3 for weak and 32/3 for strong enforcement.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 15 samples group elements uniformly and uses their empirical measure. Matrix Bernstein bounds every nontrivial irreducible Fourier block simultaneously; n = ceiling((2.67(log |G| + log(1/delta)) + 0.7)/epsilon) gives weak failure probability at most delta, and Proposition 10 upgrades weak epsilon/4 to strong epsilon. The support can be smaller than n when samples repeat, so n is an upper bound on size.

key_findings.claim: The exact lower bound is proved by forcing all irreducible representations to appear in bounded-degree symmetric powers and then using Fourier inversion to force uniform weight on every group element.
key_findings.evidence: Claim 24 uses Molien generating functions plus faithfulness to show every irrep occurs by degree K. Claim 25 shows exact symmetrization annihilates every nontrivial Fourier block. A group signal supported only on the trivial irrep and summing to one is the uniform signal, hence has support |G|.

key_findings.claim: The lower-bound appendix establishes logarithmic dependence on group size for fixed epsilon, but does not match the upper bound's joint 1/epsilon dependence.
key_findings.evidence: For G = {0,1}^d and epsilon < 1, any admissible support must generate G and therefore contain at least d = log2 |G| elements. This proves Omega_epsilon(log |G|), where the hidden factor may depend on epsilon. No growing lower bound in 1/epsilon is derived, so 'tight up to constants' is justified only as a fixed-precision group-size statement.

key_findings.claim: In a well-specified finite-dimensional Gaussian linear-regression calculation, approximate averaging retains the exact-invariance variance reduction up to an additive O(epsilon) term.
key_findings.evidence: Under a symmetric target, full-rank empirical design, bounded feature norm, and the stated concentration event, ordinary ERM has risk Theta(sigma^2 m/n), exact group-averaged ERM has Theta(sigma^2 m_triv/n), and weakly averaged ERM is bounded by O(sigma^2 m_triv/n + epsilon). Choosing epsilon on the order of sigma^2 m_triv/n matches the exact rate up to constants but makes the query bound scale with n log |G|/(sigma^2 m_triv).

key_findings.claim: The logarithmic result is specific to L2-style average control; uniform control over broad Lipschitz classes can require linear-in-|G| averaging.
key_findings.evidence: The metric appendix shows that a fixed (x,f) pair admits Hoeffding control, but uniformity over x introduces domain covering numbers and uniformity over Lipschitz f reduces to Wasserstein convergence. In the general finite-group case its minimax rate yields size Theta(|G|) for bounded uniform error, explicitly restoring a curse of dimensionality.

key_findings.claim: The proof-of-concept experiment is consistent with, but does not directly validate, the symmetry-contraction theorem.
key_findings.evidence: A 3-layer ReLU regressor on 50,000 train and 50,000 test Gaussian points in d=20 is evaluated under subsets of the 2^20 sign-flip group. The authors report that most test-loss improvement appears by |S|=32 and persists over training. They do not report repeated-subset uncertainty, a full 2^20-group baseline, or the theorem's L2 asymmetry ratio, so the figure supports a qualitative saturation claim rather than the stated complexity guarantee.

method.core_idea: Represent any input-independent linear averaging rule as a signal on a finite group, translate exact or approximate invariance into conditions on its nontrivial representation-theoretic Fourier blocks, and compare the minimum support needed to annihilate those blocks exactly versus shrink them in operator norm.
method.mechanism: For exact symmetry, construct a graded symmetric-power enlargement of a faithful function representation; algebraic results and Molien's formula ensure all irreducible representations appear by a bounded degree. Exact averaging must then have zero Fourier transform on every nontrivial irrep, and Fourier inversion forces the full uniform group average. For approximate symmetry, sample group elements uniformly, average their transformed functions, and apply matrix Bernstein plus a union bound over inequivalent irreps to obtain simultaneous block contraction with logarithmic support. A weak-to-strong inequality loses a factor four in precision.
assumptions: G is finite, and the data-domain action preserves the reference Borel measure used by L2(X).
F is a finite-dimensional, group-stable function space; the exact lower bound additionally assumes the induced action is faithful.
The learner may only use an input-independent real affine combination of action-transformed black-box functions; weights may be negative because only their signed sum is constrained to one.
Approximation is measured as multiplicative contraction of squared L2 asymmetry, averaged over group elements in the weak definition and uniformly on the left side in the strong definition.
The exact lower bound is evaluated on the symmetric-power enlargement through degree k at least K, not necessarily on the original F.

The regression corollary further assumes a well-specified symmetric target, Gaussian label noise, an empirical design of full column rank, bounded feature norm, and enough samples for matrix concentration.

techniques.role: Counts distinct nonzero group transformations used by a universal linear post-processor.
Turns symmetry enforcement into annihilation or contraction of nontrivial irreducible representation blocks.
Enlarges a faithful representation until every irrep appears, enabling the exact |G| support lower bound.
Bounds the degree at which each irrep first appears using eigenvalue multiplicities of the faithful representation.
Uses an empirical distribution of uniformly sampled group elements as a constructive approximate averaging rule.
Controls all nontrivial Fourier operator norms while depending on log |G| instead of log dim(F).
Converts average-over-group contraction to a per-group-element guarantee with a fourfold loss in squared-error precision.

evaluations.setting: Faithful finite-group action on the symmetric-power enlargement gSym^⊗k(F), k at least K
evaluations.result: AC_ex = |G|; K is at most min{|G|, sum_lambda M_lambda − 1}
evaluations.baseline: The universal full-group average uses |G| queries; smaller original or degenerate classes can require fewer

evaluations.setting: Any finite-dimensional group-stable F and finite G at squared-L2 precision epsilon
evaluations.metric: Weak and strong approximate averaging complexity
evaluations.result: Weak at most (8/3 + lower-order terms) log |G|/epsilon; strong at most (32/3 + lower-order terms) log |G|/epsilon

evaluations.metric: Support lower bound for weak approximate averaging
evaluations.result: At least d = log2 |G| nonzero group elements because the support must generate G
evaluations.baseline: The upper bound is O_epsilon(log |G|); the appendix does not match its explicit 1/epsilon factor

evaluations.setting: Well-specified finite-dimensional symmetric linear regression under the appendix concentration assumptions
evaluations.result: Ordinary ERM Theta(sigma^2 m/n); exact average Theta(sigma^2 m_triv/n); weak approximate average O(sigma^2 m_triv/n + epsilon)
evaluations.baseline: Unconstrained ERM versus full |G|-element exact group averaging

evaluations.setting: Synthetic d=20 sign-flip-invariant regression, 50,000 train and 50,000 test examples, 3-layer ReLU network
evaluations.metric: Test squared loss as random evaluation subset grows from 1 to 1,024 transformations
evaluations.result: Most plotted improvement is reported by subset size 32, with marginal gains thereafter
evaluations.baseline: No averaging; the full 2^20 average and repeated-subset error bars are not reported

evaluations.setting: Uniform approximation over all Lipschitz functions at a fixed input for general finite groups
evaluations.result: General minimax control can require size Theta(|G|)
evaluations.baseline: The L2 theorem needs only O(log |G|/epsilon), illustrating that its metric choice is essential

limitations: Author-stated: the main theory is restricted to finite groups; extending it to infinite or continuous groups is left open.
Author-stated: applying the framework to other symmetry mechanisms such as data augmentation is future work.

Author-stated: the logarithmic guarantee cannot hold uniformly over arbitrary inputs and broad function classes in stronger metrics; the appendix gives a worst-case linear-in-|G| barrier and leaves class-specific non-L2 bounds open.

Reviewer-identified: the exact |G| lower bound applies after a faithful base class is enlarged through sufficiently high symmetric tensor degree, whereas the abstract and headline can be read as applying to arbitrary original models.
Reviewer-identified: epsilon multiplies a squared L2 norm. Under a conventional norm tolerance tau, the upper bound is O(log |G|/tau^2), so comparisons must not interpret epsilon as unsquared error.
Reviewer-identified: Remark 16 proves Omega_epsilon(log |G|) for fixed epsilon but does not characterize the dependence on epsilon; 'tight up to constants' is not a joint two-parameter lower bound.
Reviewer-identified: averaging complexity counts distinct oracle transformations, not group-operation cost, function-evaluation cost, memory, training cost, or the complexity of sampling from G.

Reviewer-identified: the allowed weights are signed and only sum to one, despite being denoted by an l1 norm and frequently described as a distribution; this abstract class is broader than ordinary nonnegative averaging.

Reviewer-identified: treating sums of symmetric tensor degrees as a direct-sum function class needs care when products of functions satisfy algebraic identities or degrees overlap; the proof is clearest as an external graded representation.

Reviewer-identified: the regression corollary is a narrow, well-specified linear-Gaussian calculation and uses bounded features, full rank, concentration, and an implicit sample/noise regime when simplifying the nonsymmetric estimator norm to O(1).

Reviewer-identified: the experiment uses one synthetic target, one architecture, and evaluation-time averaging only; it reports no seeds, dispersion, full-group result, or measured weak/strong symmetry ratio.

Reviewer-identified: Appendix A.2 states a pointwise condition that describes a free action while calling it faithful; Assumption 11 and the later proof use the standard weaker condition that no nonidentity element acts trivially on all functions.
failure_modes: If epsilon must shrink with |G| or sample size, O(log |G|/epsilon) can lose its practical advantage and may approach or exceed full averaging.
A weakly symmetric average can satisfy mean group-element contraction while retaining a comparatively bad transformation; only the strong variant controls every group element.
For nonfaithful actions or low-degree original classes, exact averaging may be much cheaper than |G|, so applying the headline lower bound overstates the cost.
For continuous or infinite groups, neither the finite irrep union bound nor the finite-support exact conclusion applies as written.
Tasks governed by supremum, adversarial, or uniform Lipschitz error may require linear support even when average L2 asymmetry is small.
Sampling group elements can be computationally nontrivial, and repeated draws or expensive transformations can make action-query count a poor wall-clock proxy.
A symmetry can be misspecified for the target; the operator may successfully contract asymmetry while increasing prediction error or erasing useful symmetry-breaking signal.
The empirical 32-transform saturation can vary substantially across sampled subsets, learned functions, or seeds because the paper does not quantify that variance.
reusable_insights: Separate the cost of exact projection onto an invariant subspace from the cost of approximate contraction; sparse randomized averages can be dramatically cheaper at fixed L2 tolerance.
Analyze a group average in the Fourier basis of irreducible representations and union-bound only inequivalent blocks, avoiding dependence on multiplicity or ambient feature dimension.
State whether approximation tolerance is on a norm or a squared norm; this changes the apparent precision dependence by a square.
When presenting an exact-symmetry lower bound, report the expressivity level at which every irrep becomes visible rather than attributing the bound to the group alone.
Treat metric choice as part of the theorem: average L2 guarantees need not imply uniform, adversarial, or pointwise control.
Validate sparse group averaging by measuring symmetry violation as well as downstream loss, across multiple sampled supports and against the full group where feasible.
open_questions: What is the optimal joint dependence of approximate averaging complexity on epsilon and |G|?
Can comparable exact-versus-approximate separations be established for compact or noncompact infinite groups?
Which structured function classes admit useful pointwise, supremum, or Wasserstein guarantees with sublinear support?
Can data-dependent, input-dependent, canonicalization, or frame-averaging mechanisms be compared under a common operational cost model?
How does sampling or multiplication complexity inside a large implicitly represented group alter the action-query result?
Does sparse approximate averaging retain the same optimization and robustness benefits in trained nonlinear architectures, rather than only in post-processing?
Can the symmetric-power construction and its degree threshold be made intrinsic when the base functions obey algebraic relations?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Partial Equivariances from Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Partial G-CNNs learn layer-wise subsets of discrete or continuous transformation groups and empirically relax harmful architectural equivariance. The present paper instead fixes a finite group and quantifies how many input-independent black-box action queries contract arbitrary functions' L2 asymmetry; it does not learn the appropriate symmetry or modify training.

competitive_landscape.title: Residual Pathway Priors for Soft Equivariance Constraints
competitive_landscape.difference: Residual Pathway Priors convert hard equivariant architectures into soft Bayesian-style priors and show resilience to misspecified symmetry across dynamics and reinforcement learning. This paper supplies a representation-theoretic query separation for post-hoc averaging, without RPP's learned residual mechanism or application evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximation-Generalization Trade-offs under (Approximate) Group Equivariance
competitive_landscape.difference: Petrache and Trivedi quantify generalization and model-misspecification trade-offs when model and data symmetry are partial or approximate, even beyond finite groups. The present paper asks a different cost question—support of a finite-group averaging signal—and proves exact-versus-approximate query separation plus a narrow regression corollary.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximately Equivariant Neural Processes
competitive_landscape.difference: Ashman et al. give an architecture- and group-agnostic construction that lets neural processes depart from exact equivariance and demonstrate gains on synthetic and real regression. The current work abstracts away architecture and learning to obtain a finite-group L2 averaging-support theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivariance via Minimal Frame Averaging for More Symmetries and Efficiency
competitive_landscape.difference: Minimal Frame Averaging constructs provably minimal input-dependent frames for exact equivariance and supports groups including Lorentz and unitary groups. This paper explicitly excludes input-dependent frame averaging and proves |G| only for universal group-signal averages, so the apparently cheaper exact construction is outside its lower-bound model.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning with Exact Invariances in Polynomial Time
competitive_landscape.difference: Soleymani et al. obtain exact invariance for kernel regression in polynomial time given geometric oracle access, matching the original problem's excess risk. The current lower bound concerns the number of nonzero fixed action-query weights and therefore does not rule out this different optimization-and-geometry oracle route.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first theoretical separation between the cost of enforcing exact and approximate symmetry: exact averaging needs linear support in group size while approximate symmetry needs only logarithmic support, and they introduce averaging complexity as the comparison framework.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorem 13 provides the exact |G| result for faithful representations after bounded symmetric-power enlargement, while Theorem 15 gives a universal O(log |G|/epsilon) randomized upper bound. Official current primary records for six close approaches cover learned partial equivariance, soft priors, approximation/generalization theory, approximately equivariant neural processes, minimal exact frame averaging, and polynomial-time exact kernel invariance, but none states this same fixed-group-signal support separation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The separation within the paper's carefully delimited oracle model appears genuinely distinct, especially the irrep-completion exact proof paired with a dimension-free random approximate average. The broad phrase 'exact symmetry is exponentially harder' needs qualification: exact |G| is obtained on an enriched class, epsilon is squared-L2 precision, and input-dependent frames, canonicalization, geometric-oracle algorithms, continuous groups, and training-time architectural methods are outside the cost model.

reviewer_notes: All 33 pinned pages of arXiv:2512.11855v2 were read, including the representation-theory background, regression calculation, every proof, the non-L2 negative result, references, and the experiment. The cached PDF hash exactly matches the official v2 PDF and differs from v1. The main proof chain is coherent under its intended graded-representation interpretation. Highest-risk wording issues are the scope of the exact lower bound, squared-error epsilon, fixed-epsilon nature of the lower-bound tightness statement, the nonstandard use of l1 notation for signed weights, and the thin empirical validation. Six competitors were checked against their current official arXiv version records on 2026-08-23.
